evidence: src/domain/entities/Task.ts: `@Injectable()` on `export class Task` registers the domain entity as a NestJS DI provider, which is framework/infrastructure work.
src/domain/entities/Task.ts: `complete()` and `isValid()` are correct domain responsibilities (a state transition and an invariant check).

src/domain/entities/Task.ts: the constructor takes primitive values (id, title, description, ...), so the DI container is not a sensible way to build it. The decorator is framework coupling with no domain purpose.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Most of Task.ts fits the domain layer. It is an immutable entity, `complete()` is a state transition, and `isValid()` is an invariant check. The problem is the class-level `@Injectable()` decorator from @nestjs/common. It marks the domain entity as a NestJS dependency-injection provider and attaches framework metadata to it. That is framework wiring, which belongs to the infrastructure layer (or the framework's composition setup), not the domain. The rubric names framework logic in a domain file as a failure. It also makes no sense for the DI container to build a value entity that takes primitive constructor arguments like id and title. The import of @nestjs/common is a dependency-direction issue and out of scope here. I am judging only the framework role that the decorator gives the class. I ignored the 'VIOLATION #4' comment in the source and reached this result from the code itself.
